To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) there is a systematic “food perception gap” between what people subjectively describe and how an algorithm objectively recognizes food in images, (ii) the food perception gap relates to county-level health outcomes, and (iii) the food perception is more closely related to health outcomes than what the algorithm objectively sees.

the perception gap on Instagram, measured as the difference between a machine and human label, is negatively correlated with the county’s obesity rates, and positively correlated with the county level fruit and vegetable consumption.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: “Is Saki #Delicious?”, where “Saki” is an arbitrary food item and “Delicious” is a hashtag.
the gap between the objective and subjective aspects of food images and how it relates to public health.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we are not yet sure what we are sure of.
we find a perception gap between how food is perceived by humans and how it is perceived by a machine.
we find that the perception gap is a good indicator of the health of the population, and that the perception gap varies across different types of food.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the “perception” of what we eat on social media differs from the “reality”, which is reflected in health outcomes.
we use image recognition to study how people perceive food images and how this perception is linked to their health.
we show how a large-scale analysis of food images on Instagram can be used to study the perception gap, a concept which has been shown to relate to health outcomes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are systematic differences in how we perceive food and that this can be related to health outcomes.
there is a systematic difference between how humans perceive food and how a computer perceives it, and this difference relates to health.
there is a systematic gap between how people perceive food and how it actually is, which is associated with certain health outcomes.
